title: Twenty Minutes From Waking Up: the Court's Finding on the $12 Billion Nickel Cancellation
participants: Elliott Associates L.P. and Elliott International L.P.
High Court of Justice, King's Bench Division, Divisional Court

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The profits at stake are the claimants' own figures: Elliott put its lost net profits at "about US$456 million" and Jane Street at "about US$15 million", on trades done between midnight and 08:15 on a single morning. The court observed that damages are "what really drives this litigation".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is where the short positions were held. "Tsingshan's short activity was acquired not on the LME but on the over-the-counter ('OTC') market, making it less visible to the LME." The exchange that had to judge whether its own market was orderly could not see the positions driving it, because they were not on it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The court's finding on this is the heart of the dossier, and it is a finding about ignorance rather than concealment. At paragraph 185: "Mr Chamberlain reached the conclusion that the nickel market was disorderly fairly rapidly – within about 20 minutes from waking up in the morning of 8 March 2022. He did so without speaking to or consulting anyone, on the basis of some internet research on his mobile phone and his own familiarity with the market ... However, his conclusion was not based on any real investigation. He was not aware of the fact that there were several market participants with significant short positions – despite the fact that there had been some press reports in relation to Tsingshan. He therefore did not appreciate that the immediate cause of the sharp rise in prices was the short squeeze which Tsingshan and the other relevant short traders were experiencing."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall went to the parties the decision-maker did not know existed. At 08:15 trading was suspended; at 12:05 the LME "published a notice cancelling all nickel trades entered into on that day before the Suspension". "The aggregate value of the cancelled trades was around US$12 billion." The effect was to unwind a morning's gains for the buyers and a morning's losses for the shorts — and the court found that the man who decided it "did not appreciate" that the shorts were what was happening.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment is judicial and complete: "we reject the Claimants' case that either the Cancellation Decision or the 8 March Margin Decision was unlawful"; "both Claimants' claims for judicial review fail on all grounds and their challenges are dismissed". The court held that even though Mr Chamberlain could have found out "at least something" about the squeeze, the press reports "would not have provided a very satisfactory basis", since "the true position was much more complex". It also departed from the exchange's own commissioned review on one point, saying of the Oliver Wyman report's authors: "We do not know what evidence they considered in relation to price bands."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: LME Rule TR 22, which the court held met the requirement of legal certainty because it "applies to a class comprising highly sophisticated and well-resourced commercial actors who chose to contract on LME Rules, including TR 22" — a cancellation power whose breadth is justified by the sophistication of the people it can be used against.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A judgment holding that a commercial exchange exercising regulatory functions may void $12 billion of concluded trades on a 20-minute, uninvestigated assessment without acting unlawfully, and that its users' consent to its rulebook defeats their property claim.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Positions move off-exchange to avoid visibility; invisibility means the exchange cannot diagnose its own market; the undiagnosed move is called disorderly; the cancellation power is used; and the users' prior consent to that power is what makes the cancellation unchallengeable. The court quoted Sims v Dacorum on the point: "the loss of [Mr Sims's] property right is the result of a bargain that he himself made."

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the London Metal Exchange cancelled $12 billion of trades to rescue Tsingshan and the other short sellers from a squeeze that would have destroyed them — a deliberate intervention on behalf of insiders, dressed up as market management.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The court found something that no conspiracy account predicts and which is harder to live with. The decision that the nickel market was disorderly was reached by the LME's chief executive "within about 20 minutes from waking up", "without speaking to or consulting anyone", "on the basis of some internet research on his mobile phone", and — the finding that destroys the rescue reading — "He was not aware of the fact that there were several market participants with significant short positions", so "he therefore did not appreciate that the immediate cause of the sharp rise in prices was the short squeeze which Tsingshan and the other relevant short traders were experiencing." The decision-maker could not have been protecting the shorts, because on the court's finding he did not know they were there. The court went further and accepted that he could have found out "at least something" from the press reports, but held it would not have helped, because "the true position was much more complex than the contemporary press reports suggested, and that the scale of the short squeeze was much more significant (and not confined to Tsingshan)". So the single-villain version fails twice: Tsingshan "is the only short identified by name in the OW Report", but that report "makes it clear that there were several such participants". The challenges were dismissed on all grounds. And Elliott lost before the merits were reached on its property claim, for a reason entirely about plumbing: its trades "were not fully cleared", so they were "Contingent Agreements to Trade" that "did not result in Client Contracts" and therefore were not "possessions" at all, while Jane Street's concluded contracts were. WHAT IS NOT SETTLED HERE: this judgment is "not concerned with the claims for damages", which were split off to a separate hearing; the Oliver Wyman report itself was not read, only the court's references to it; and no finding is made anywhere that the LME acted in order to protect any short.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: R (Elliott Associates L.P. and Elliott International L.P.) v The London Metal Exchange and LME Clear Ltd, and R (Jane Street Global Trading LLC) v the same, [2023] EWHC 2969 (Admin), Divisional Court, 29 November 2023. It records: a pronounced nickel price spike early on 8 March 2022; suspension of nickel trading at 08:15; a notice at 12:05 cancelling all nickel trades entered into that day before the suspension; cancelled trades of around US$12 billion aggregate value; claimed lost net profits of about US$456 million (Elliott) and about US$15 million (Jane Street); Tsingshan's short built on the OTC market and so less visible to the LME, though covered in the financial press in the days before; the chief executive's conclusion of disorderliness reached within about 20 minutes of waking, unconsulted, on mobile internet research, not based on any real investigation, and without awareness that several participants held significant short positions or that a short squeeze was the immediate cause; the court's acceptance that something could have been found out but its holding that press reports would not have been a satisfactory basis because the true position was more complex and the squeeze larger and not confined to Tsingshan; Tsingshan as the only short named in the Oliver Wyman report, which nonetheless identifies several; Jane Street's trades as concluded contracts constituting possessions and Elliott's as uncleared Contingent Agreements to Trade that did not; rejection of the case that either the Cancellation Decision or the 8 March Margin Decision was unlawful; dismissal of the A1P1 claims; and dismissal of both claims for judicial review on all grounds.

citations.title: R (Elliott Associates L.P. & Elliott International L.P.) v The London Metal Exchange & LME Clear Ltd; R (Jane Street Global Trading, LLC) v same [2023] EWHC 2969 (Admin), Divisional Court (Swift J and Bright J), 29 November 2023
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on the National Archives' Find Case Law service, which is the official publisher of judgments of the courts of England and Wales. THE EVENTS, AS FOUND: "In early March 2022, nickel prices rose very dramatically. There was a particularly pronounced spike early in the morning of 8 March 2022. At 08:15 on that day, the LME suspended nickel trading ('the Suspension'). At 12:05, the LME published a notice cancelling all nickel trades entered into on that day before the Suspension ('the Cancellation')." "The aggregate value of the cancelled trades was around US$12 billion." Elliott claimed the Cancellation cost it "net profits totalling about US$456 million"; Jane Street "about US$15 million". THE OUTCOME: "we reject the Claimants' case that either the Cancellation Decision or the 8 March Margin Decision was unlawful" (paragraph 217); "we dismiss the A1P1 claims" (paragraph 250); "both Claimants' claims for judicial review fail on all grounds and their challenges are dismissed" (paragraph 251). THE FINDING THAT DISPLACES THE CONSPIRACY READING, AND REPLACES IT WITH SOMETHING ELSE. At paragraph 185: "Mr Chamberlain reached the conclusion that the nickel market was disorderly fairly rapidly – within about 20 minutes from waking up in the morning of 8 March 2022. He did so without speaking to or consulting anyone, on the basis of some internet research on his mobile phone and his own familiarity with the market, including the events of the previous few days. His conclusion was then tested and confirmed in the course of the two remote meetings that followed at 07:30 and 09:00. However, his conclusion was not based on any real investigation. He was not aware of the fact that there were several market participants with significant short positions – despite the fact that there had been some press reports in relation to Tsingshan. He therefore did not appreciate that the immediate cause of the sharp rise in prices was the short squeeze which Tsingshan and the other relevant short traders were experiencing." The court accepted at paragraph 189 that "in the limited time available, it would have been possible for Mr Chamberlain to find out at least something about the involvement of a short squeeze affecting some market participants, notably Tsingshan", but held at paragraph 190 that the press reports "would not have provided a very satisfactory basis", because "the true position was much more complex than the contemporary press reports suggested, and that the scale of the short squeeze was much more significant (and not confined to Tsingshan)". ON TSINGSHAN AND VISIBILITY: "Tsingshan's short activity was acquired not on the LME but on the over-the-counter ('OTC') market, making it less visible to the LME. However, a number of reports in the financial press in the days leading up to 8 March 2022 covered Tsingshan's short position." And on the Oliver Wyman report commissioned afterwards: "Tsingshan is the only short identified by name in the OW Report. However, while the OW Report confirms that most of the buying activity over the relevant days was driven by participants exposed to large short positions, it makes it clear that there were several such participants." ON WHY THE PROPERTY CLAIM FAILED, which is a point about the plumbing: Jane Street's trades "gave rise to concluded contracts that constituted 'possessions'", but the Elliott claimants' trades "were not fully cleared" and so "were Contingent Agreements to Trade" that "did not result in Client Contracts" — they lost on the possession test before reaching the merits of their A1P1 claim. The court also relied on the claimants' own consent to LME Rule TR 22, quoting Sims v Dacorum Borough Council: "the loss of [Mr Sims's] property right is the result of a bargain that he himself made." WHAT THE JUDGMENT DOES NOT DECIDE: it "is not concerned with the claims for damages", which were split off; the Oliver Wyman report itself was not read for this dossier, only the court's references to it; and the court expressly departed from that report on one point — "we are reaching a different view of the significance of price bands from that of the authors of the OW Report. We do not know what evidence they considered in relation to price bands". No finding is made anywhere in this judgment that the LME acted in order to protect Tsingshan or any other short, and none is asserted here.
